hops.title: Blindfolded volunteers following a chocolate trail
hops.text: In 2007, Jess Porter, Noam Sobel and colleagues gave volunteers blindfolds, earplugs and gloves, set them down in an open grassy field and asked them to follow a chocolate-scented trail by smell alone. Two-thirds of them managed it, noses close to the grass, and four volunteers who kept practicing got faster. Part of the trick is that your two nostrils sample air about 3.5 centimeters apart. When the researchers routed both nostrils into one shared input, so left and right could no longer be compared, tracking got harder. A growth cone in the collagen gel has the same job: it finds a direction by comparing one side with the other.

sources.citation: Porter et al., Nature Neuroscience 10:27-29 (2007), PMID 17173046.
Raithel & Gottfried, Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews (2021), PMID 34214515 / PMC8359807.

hops.afterHeading: The worm already knew: one cue, two readers
hops.title: One earthy smell that repels flies and attracts mosquitoes
hops.text: It is easy to assume a smell carries its own meaning, pleasant or foul. Geosmin, the molecule behind the earthy smell of wet soil and beetroot, says otherwise. To a fruit fly it is an alarm for harmful microbes: it activates one dedicated circuit that drives the fly away and suppresses feeding and egg laying. The same molecule draws a yellow fever mosquito to lay her eggs nearby, probably because it signals microbes her larvae eat. Pure geosmin is expensive, so in 2020 researchers in northeastern Brazil baited recycled plastic bottles with beetroot peel extract, where geosmin concentrates. Those traps collected significantly more mosquito eggs than bottles of plain water.

sources.citation: Melo et al., Current Biology 30(1):127-134.e5 (2020), PMID 31839454 / PMC7144812.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A strip of beetroot peel beside a small dish of water, with a fruit fly flying away on one side and a mosquito approaching from the other.
image.caption: The same earthy molecule drives fruit flies away and draws egg-laying mosquitoes in; the reader decides.

hops.afterHeading: The vertebrate readers: DCC and UNC5
hops.title: Mirror movements in people and hopping kanga mice
hops.text: Most of us can make a fist with one hand while the other lies flat on the desk. People born with certain mutations in DCC, or in NTN1, the gene for netrin-1, can have congenital mirror movements: a deliberate movement of one hand is echoed involuntarily by the other, which makes typing hard. In affected people, more of the tract carrying movement commands stays on the same side instead of crossing the midline, likely letting commands reach both hands. Mice with two copies of a Dcc mutation nicknamed kanga hop like rabbits, both hind legs pushing off together. Removing Dcc from just the spinal cord makes mice hop too.

audio.title: Beetroot traps, hopping mice and trapped immune cells
audio.transcript:
A cue is only half a message. The cell that reads it supplies the rest. Here are three places outside an embryonic spinal cord where that idea shows up.

Start with the smell of wet soil after rain, a molecule called geosmin. You might think a smell has one fixed meaning, good or bad, built into its chemistry. Not at all. In a fruit fly, geosmin activates a dedicated circuit that warns of harmful microbes and suppresses feeding and egg laying. Now offer the exact same molecule to a yellow fever mosquito. She prefers to lay her eggs near it, probably because geosmin comes from microbes, like the ones her larvae eat. In two thousand twenty, researchers spotted something wonderfully practical here. Pure geosmin is expensive, but it is the compound that gives beetroot its earthy smell, and it is concentrated in the peel. So the team painted recycled plastic bottles black, baited them with beetroot peel extract on a university campus in northeastern Brazil, and collected significantly more mosquito eggs than water traps did. Same molecule, opposite verdict. The reader sets the sign.

Next, what happens in people when the netrin pathway itself is altered. In two thousand ten, geneticists studying a French Canadian family and an Iranian family found that mutations in D C C cause congenital mirror movements. Seven years later, in two thousand seventeen, a larger collaboration found the same condition in people carrying mutations in N T N one, the gene for netrin one itself. For people born with mirror movements, making a fist with one hand makes the other hand echo the motion involuntarily, so tasks like typing, which need the two hands to move differently, get harder. Studies of affected people point to movement-command axons that did not cross the midline in the usual way during development. Mice show a striking echo of this. A spontaneous D C C mutation that turned up in a mouse colony in Maine was nicknamed kanga, after the kangaroo-like hop of adult mice carrying two copies; they hop on both hind feet together, like rabbits. Later work showed that removing D C C only in the mouse spinal cord misroutes commissural axons and is enough to produce that hopping gait.

And netrin one does not retire once the nervous system is built. In two thousand twelve, researchers studying artery plaques in humans and mice found that cholesterol-stuffed immune cells called macrophages, sitting inside those plaques, make netrin one themselves. Acting through the repulsive receptor U N C five B, that netrin one blocks the macrophages from migrating toward the chemical cues that would lead them out, trapping them in the artery wall and keeping the inflammation going. When scientists gave plaque-prone mice blood-forming cells that lacked netrin one, so their macrophages lacked it too, more macrophages left the plaques, and the mice developed much less atherosclerosis.

Geosmin sends fruit flies away and draws egg-laying yellow fever mosquitoes in. Netrin one helps wire the circuits for movement and, years later, can keep macrophages stuck in artery plaques. Over and over, what a cue does depends on who is reading it.
